title: The Destruction of Chmielnik’s Jews: Encirclement, Selections and Deportation
summary: The deportations and killings are the defining rupture in the community’s history and deserve a careful account grounded in survivor testimony.

editorialContent:
![Chmielnik, the town whose Jewish community was destroyed](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Market_Square_in_Chmielnik_%283%29.jpg/1920px-Market_Square_in_Chmielnik_%283%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A town transformed into a ghetto

Before the war, Jews made up about four-fifths of Chmielnik’s population. By the end of 1941, the ghetto held roughly 9,000 people, including refugees driven there from surrounding towns and western Poland. German authorities had confined Jewish residents there in April 1941, forbidding them to leave. The independent account of Yad Vashem describes a crowded community already shaped by forced labor, poverty and a typhus epidemic. Its history supplies the setting for the [Chmielnik ghetto](/communities/chmielnik/records/mention_a34f3b9aa2e7d76d4dca53b8): a place of coerced confinement, but also of communal institutions and daily efforts to survive. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406))

The memorial book, *Pinkes Khmielnik*, preserves the event through different witnesses and accounts. Its record of the [mass deportation from the town](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_7654f8c0b66df0ee8258e213) describes people robbed, assembled and driven to Khentshin, where they were loaded into cattle wagons. Other supplied records focus on particular stages of the destruction: the roundup of men, the burning of the Great Synagogue, and the deportation of young people to forced labor. Taken together, they show that the community’s destruction was not one isolated action, but a sequence of escalating measures.

## Forced labor and the first removal

Work was used both to exploit Jews and to encourage the belief that being useful might offer protection. Yad Vashem reports that Germans established workshops for war production and that officials assured ghetto residents that those who continued working would survive. In reality, selection and deportation proceeded alongside labor. On October 1, 1942, about 1,200 young people were sent to an ammunition factory at Skarżysko-Kamienna; a further 40 went to a labor camp in Kielce. The [deportation of young people to forced labor](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_35051fdd20e6ce7f59bb5e1e) is recorded in the memorial material, while Yad Vashem independently gives similar figures and destinations. These records establish the destination of the selected group, but do not tell us the individual fate of every young person sent away. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406))

The removals came amid growing danger. On October 3, Yad Vashem says, 1,270 Jews expelled from nearby communities arrived in Chmielnik. Two days later, German forces surrounded the ghetto. The memorial book’s account of the [search and seizure of Jewish men](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_6e7381efb0313b3b21f6b5dc) describes Germans searching homes, taking hundreds of men and gathering them along Busk Road. Such episodes remind us that people were not simply transported from a single assembly point: homes and streets were entered, families divided, and those unable to keep pace faced lethal danger.

## October 5 and 6: the main deportation

The records distinguish between encirclement on October 5 and the deportation action on October 6. The memorial book has a record for the [encirclement of the Chmielnik ghetto](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_b21ff242b6f494c0ab2bcf47), naming gendarmerie and other forces, and a separate account of the [Chmielnik deportation action](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_c833faf85191d4b22922bd96), dated October 6. The wider record confirms the sequence: Yad Vashem names SS forces under Hans Gaier, assisted by Ukrainian, Lithuanian and Latvian auxiliaries, as surrounding the ghetto on October 5, with the violent action following the next day. The memorial book also identifies gendarmes, SS personnel, Ukrainian and Polish police, and firefighters among the forces connected with the encirclement. The accounts do not describe every unit’s exact role in each phase, so those distinctions should not be flattened into a single, overly precise description. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406))

The book’s account of the [Great Synagogue set on fire](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_13b5eccef376a3e5122fa2ad) adds a stark local scene: German forces set the building alight, and men fleeing it were shot. A separate family memorial names Samuel Vayechniak, his wife Rachel and their two children as having died in Chmielnik during the expulsion on October 6. These names bring the violence into the scale of a household: not an anonymous crowd, but parents and children whose fate was remembered by the community. The record does not provide further biographical detail, and the evidence here does not establish whether they died in the synagogue episode or elsewhere during the action.

Numbers differ across accounts. The memorial book’s event summary says about 11,000 people were assembled, robbed and driven to Khentshin. Yad Vashem gives a lower figure—about 8,500 Jews taken to Chełciny (Chęciny), about 45 kilometres away—and says hundreds were shot on the way, while about 500 more were murdered in the ghetto during the action. The difference may reflect differing estimates, who was counted, or the inclusion of people gathered from outside the town; the available evidence does not resolve it. The place names Khentshin and Chełciny refer in these accounts to the stated assembly destination. At Khentshin, according to the book’s transport account, people were loaded into cattle cars and deported to Treblinka. Yad Vashem likewise records that those who reached the destination were deported to Treblinka. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406))

## Those left behind—and the next roundup

The first action did not immediately end Jewish life in Chmielnik. Yad Vashem reports that Germans left 72 Jews in the ghetto building of the Jewish Council, assigning them to bury the dead. Hundreds who had hidden in nearby forests joined them within days, forming a small ghetto of around 700 people. Its account says a second action began on November 5: most residents were sent toward Stopnica, while 75 remained after selection. Many deportees escaped along the way and attempted to hide. The memorial book’s record of the [second resettlement from Chmielnik](/communities/chmielnik/records/event_candidate_0b8a936a0ee43acccbc28319) also places it on November 5–6 and says most were sent toward Stopnica on peasant wagons. The sources differ in how they describe the transport and exact sequence; neither account supports treating every person’s route or fate as known. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406))

The later fate of those who escaped is a thread the records leave open. Yad Vashem says many tried to survive in hiding after fleeing the November deportation, but its Chmielnik entry does not identify them individually. The memorial book’s contents show that survivors later wrote about hiding, life on the “Aryan side,” forced labor in Kielce and Skarżysko, and partisan activity in the region. Those chapters reveal the range of routes survivors took, but the supplied evidence does not connect each account to a particular escape from the November action. The town’s [Busk Road] and the [forests around Chmielnik] remain promising avenues for tracing the local geography of roundup and escape.

Yad Vashem records a final liquidation action on December 20, 1942, when nearly all remaining residents were deported toward Sandomierz. This wider chronology makes clear that the October deportation, devastating as it was, was not the last act in the destruction of Jewish life in the town. The memorial book’s layered testimony—its different dates, estimates, family names and scenes—preserves what survivors and relatives could remember. The independent record helps check and extend that memory, but it cannot restore every name or settle every discrepancy. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=406))
